cite: Rowland v. Miller, 54 N.Y. St. Rep. 465

cite: Siegman v. Keeler, 54 N.Y. St. Rep. 125
court: New York Court of Common Pleas
holding_summary: A boarding house keeper is not an insurer of a boarder's goods the way an innkeeper is of a guest's; she is liable for loss of a boarder's property only upon a failure to exercise ordinary care in admitting patrons and safeguarding the premises. Finding no evidence of such negligence, the court reversed the plaintiff's judgment and ordered a new trial.

quotes.text: a boarding-house keeper is answerable for a loss of the goods only if he has omitted to exercise ordinary care to prevent it.

notes: Tort/bailment case, not a letting-rights case per se, but doctrinally characterizes the boarder/boarding-house-keeper relation as legally distinct from innkeeper/guest and treats boarding as an ordinary lawful business subject to ordinary-care standards rather than insurer liability.

court: New York City Court, General Term
holding_summary: In an action by a boarding house keeper for breach of a contract to furnish board and lodging to forty-five convention delegates, the court treated her claim as a meritorious, enforceable business contract, but reversed for a new trial because the correct measure of damages is the plaintiff's actual loss from the breach, not the agreed contract price.

quotes.text: The plaintiff, a boarding house keeper, agreed to furnish board and lodging to forty-five persons to be sent to her house by the committee of the Eleventh International Christian Endeavor Convention, of which the defendant was treasurer.
The claim seems to be a meritorious one, and ought to be discharged in a practical manner by its payment.

The true measure of damages by a boarding house keeper against those engaging board and lodging and not taking the agreed accommodations, is not what the parties agreed to pay, but what the plaintiff lost in consequence of the breach.

holding_summary: Where a boarding house keeper seized a departing boarder's effects to secure an unpaid board bill exceeding their value, the court held her lien over the boarder's goods valid and, applying an innkeeper's-lien analogy, enforceable even against property otherwise exempt from levy and sale on execution; judgment for the defendant boarding house keeper was affirmed.
